title: Weeping at Bochim and the Pattern of the Judges
summary: The angel of the LORD rebukes Israel at Bochim for making peace with the Canaanites and announces that those peoples will remain as thorns and their gods as a snare, and the people weep. The narrator then looks back to Joshua's death and forward over the whole period: a new generation grows up not knowing the LORD, serves the Baals, and falls under oppressors, and God, moved by their groaning, raises up judges to save them, only for Israel to fall back further each time.
story: Chapter 1 told the story of the unfinished conquest from the outside; chapter 2 tells it from God's point of view. It is the key to the whole book. The first scene (verses 1 to 5) explains the failures of chapter 1 as disobedience. The second (verses 6 to 10) steps back to Joshua's death, repeating Joshua 24:28-31 almost word for word, to mark the turn from one generation to the next. The third (verses 11 to 23) lays out, in advance, the cycle that the rest of the book will fill with names: Othniel, Ehud, Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah, Samson. When you read those stories, this chapter is the frame the narrator wants you to see them in.
historical:
The chapter surveys the whole period of the judges rather than one moment, roughly the two centuries or so between Joshua and the rise of Saul, however that period is dated. Its first scene moves from Gilgal, Israel's first camp after crossing the Jordan and a place of covenant memory (Joshua 4 and 5), to Bochim, a place not otherwise known; the ancient Greek translation connects it with Bethel, which was near. The name means weepers, and it is given because of what happened there.

Joshua's burial place is called Timnath-heres here and Timnath-serah in Joshua 19:50 and 24:30. The two names differ by the order of their letters. Heres is a word for the sun, and some scholars think one form was altered to avoid or to reflect a link with sun worship, while others see a simple scribal variation. The location is the same, in the hill country of Ephraim.
cultural:
Baal was the great god of Canaanite religion, the storm god who was believed to bring rain and so the fertility of fields, flocks, and families. Texts discovered at Ugarit, on the Syrian coast, in the late 1920s describe his battles and his death and return to life, which the Canaanites connected with the dry and rainy seasons. The plural Baals (verse 11) probably refers to the many local forms of the god worshiped at different shrines. The Ashtoreths were forms of Astarte, a goddess linked with fertility and war. For a farming people who depended on rain in a land without great rivers, these gods offered what seemed a practical guarantee of survival. Serving them didn't feel like apostasy; it felt like good farming.

The judges (verse 16) were not mainly courtroom figures, though Deborah did settle disputes. The Hebrew word describes someone who puts things right, and in this book the judges are chiefly deliverers: military leaders raised up by God to free Israel from oppressors, who then led the tribes during their lifetime. Being gathered to one's fathers (verse 10) was a way of speaking of death and burial with one's ancestors.
literary: The chapter has three parts: a prophetic rebuke (1 to 5), a flashback to Joshua's death (6 to 10), and a theological summary (11 to 23). The summary sets out the cycle that will shape the book: Israel does evil and serves other gods; the LORD's anger burns and he hands them over to plunderers; they are distressed; the LORD raises up judges who save them; the judge dies and they fall further. Later stories add a crying out to the LORD, which this summary implies in the groaning of verse 18. The phrase "did evil in the sight of the LORD" (verse 11) becomes a refrain that opens each new cycle. Notice that verse 19 describes a downward spiral rather than a circle: each generation becomes even more corrupt than their fathers. The chapter ends with a double explanation for why the nations remain: as judgment (verse 21) and as a test (verse 22).

outline.t: The angel of the LORD rebukes Israel at Bochim
Joshua dies, and a generation arises that does not know the LORD
Israel serves the Baals and is handed to plunderers
The LORD raises judges, and Israel keeps falling back
The nations are left to test Israel

doctrines.note: Israel forsakes the God who brought them out of Egypt and serves the gods of the peoples around them. The chapter traces idolatry to forgetting: a generation that did not know the LORD or his works.
God's anger burns against covenant-breaking, and he hands his people over to their enemies. Judgment here is not arbitrary; it is the covenant's own warning, as he had sworn to them (verse 15).
The LORD is moved to pity by Israel's groaning (verse 18). His mercy is the reason the cycle doesn't end in destruction, even though the people's repentance is shallow.

Verse 10 is one of Scripture's starkest warnings about the passing on of faith. The generation that saw God's works did not ensure that their children knew him, despite the commands of Deuteronomy 6:6-9.

words.note: Yada, to know. It means more than having information; it often means knowing by experience and relationship. The new generation did not know the LORD or the works he had done (verse 10). They may have heard the stories, but they did not know him.

Shaphat, to judge, and the source of the book's title. The word covers governing, deciding cases, and putting wrongs right. In Judges it mostly describes leaders who rescue Israel from oppression and then lead the tribes.
Yasha, to save or deliver. It is the root of the names Joshua and Jesus. The judges save Israel from those who plunder them (verse 16), though the saving is God's: he raises them up and is with them.

Nacham, to be sorry, to be moved to pity or to relent. Verse 18 says the LORD was moved by their groaning. The word shows a God whose heart is engaged by his people's suffering, even when they have brought it on themselves.

christ: The judges were saviors raised up by God, with God present in them, who rescued Israel for a while. Each died, and the rescue faded. The chapter's own logic leaves the reader looking for a deliverer who does not die and a rescue that changes the people from within. The New Testament presents Jesus as that savior, whose very name comes from the same root as the verb in verse 16, and whose resurrection means that his saving work doesn't end at his death (Hebrews 7:23-25). The angel of the LORD, who speaks here as God himself (I brought you up out of Egypt), has been read by many Christian interpreters as an appearance of the Son before his incarnation; others read him as a created messenger who speaks with God's full authority. The broader link is thematic: Judges shows why a better savior was needed.

hard.q: If God could have driven out the nations, why did he leave them to test and punish Israel?
hard.a: The chapter gives two reasons that sit together. First, the nations remain as judgment: Israel made covenants with them and did not tear down their altars, so God gives them what they chose (verses 2 and 3, 20 and 21). Second, they remain as a test, to show whether Israel would keep the LORD's way (verse 22), and 3:2 adds that it taught a new generation how to fight. Some readers find it troubling that God would allow a situation in which his people were likely to fail. Others see in it the seriousness of a covenant: God does not force faithfulness, and he lets his people face the consequences of their choices while still coming to their rescue. The chapter holds both God's justice and his mercy without resolving every tension between them.

questions: Verse 10 says a whole generation grew up not knowing the LORD. What helps faith pass from one generation to the next, and what gets in the way?
The people wept at Bochim, but their behavior didn't change for long. What is the difference between sorrow over sin and real change?
Baal promised rain and harvests. What do people today trust to secure their livelihood in a way that competes with trust in God?
